bib.title: A Comprehensive Survey of Self-Evolving AI Agents: A New Paradigm Bridging Foundation Models and Lifelong Agentic Systems

legacy_report:
SOURCE: A Comprehensive Survey of Self-Evolving AI Agents: A New Paradigm Bridging Foundation Models and Lifelong Agentic Systems. Jinyuan Fang, Yanwen Peng, Xi Zhang et al. (Glasgow, Sheffield, MBZUAI, others; corresponding author Zaiqiao Meng). arXiv:2508.07407v2, 31 Aug 2025. Preprint.

COVERAGE: Read chars 0-153,587 of 246,967 in full (body, sections 1-9, conclusions). Chars 153,587-end are the reference list, skimmed only for origins. There are no appendices with results. Extraction was clean. The extracted text is at /tmp/fang.txt if you need to re-quote.

NOTE ON FIT: This is a taxonomy survey with essentially no new measurements. Nearly every number in the text is a cited system's result or a count of laws or stages. The note's practitioner evolve loop (5-10 run cadence, anti-busywork) has no counterpart here. I found no mention of "no change needed", of rewriting config files or SOPs, or of cadence. The note already lists a different survey, Ren et al. 2607.13104, and not this one. Fang is not in the note's source list, and grep found no "fang" or 2508.07407 in it.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: The survey defines self-evolving agents and gives the loop four components (System Inputs, Agent System, Environment, Optimiser). The optimiser is a search space plus an algorithm that maximises a scalar score.
  number: none (formula A* = argmax_{A in S} O(A; I))
  setup: Conceptual framework, Section 3. The loop stops when a performance threshold or convergence is reached. The optimiser may also synthesise training examples to grow the inputs.
  quote: "The loop terminates once a predefined performance threshold is reached or convergence criteria are satisfied." and "An optimiser is typically defined by two core components: (1)search space (S)... (2)optimisation algorithm (H)"
  where: p.10-12, ~chars 27,500-33,000

- claim: It proposes "Three Laws" as ordered constraints: Endure (safety and stability during any modification), then Excel (preserve or improve existing performance), then Evolve (optimise autonomously).
  number: 3 laws, strictly prioritised
  setup: Normative proposal. No empirical test.
  quote: "Subject to the First law, self-evolving AI agents must preserve or enhance existing task performance;"
  where: p.3, ~chars 4,500

- claim: The survey places the field on a four-stage path: MOP (offline pretraining), MOA (online adaptation), MAO (multi-agent orchestration), MASE (multi-agent self-evolving). It says full autonomy is still far off.
  number: 4 paradigms
  setup: Framing, Section 1.
  quote: "Despite self-evolving AI agents representing an ambitious vision for future AI systems, achieving this level of autonomy remains a long-term goal. Current systems are still far from exhibiting the full capabilities required for safe, robust and open-ended self-evolution."
  where: p.3

- claim: Safety evaluation of evolving agents is the unsolved part. Existing evaluations are snapshots. Each evolution step must be assessed for unintended or malicious behaviour, and longitudinal, evolution-aware benchmarks do not yet exist.
  number: none
  setup: Section 7.3.
  quote: "Despite these advances, most current evaluations aresnapshot-based, assessing agents at a single point in time." and "Developing longitudinal, evolution-aware benchmarks that track safety, alignment, and robustness across the full lifecycle of an agent ecosystem remains an open and urgent challenge."
  where: p.32, ~chars 147,500

- claim: Optimised prompts and topologies are brittle across backbones.
  number: none
  setup: Section 8.1.2, stated as an open challenge, not measured.
  quote: "Optimised prompts or agent topologies are often brittle, showing poor generalisation across LLM backbones with differing reasoning abilities."
  where: p.33

- claim: Reward and feedback signals for evolution are unreliable. Learned step-level reward models are noisy and unstable. Domains without ground truth make feedback untrustworthy.
  number: none
  setup: Section 8.1.1 and 8.1.2.
  quote: "Learned reward models for intermediate reasoning steps often suffer from dataset scarcity, noisy supervision, and feedback inconsistency, leading to unstable or divergent agent behaviours." and "In domains like biomedicine or law, reliable ground truth is often absent or disputed"
  where: p.33

- claim: Where a verifiable signal exists (compiler, unit tests, proof assistant), evolution works by filtering self-generated trajectories. Process reward models are said to beat outcome-only feedback. The survey gives no numbers for this.
  number: none
  setup: Sections 4.1 and 4.1.2. Cited systems include STaR, NExT, DeepSeek-Prover, DeepSeek-R1 with GRPO.
  quote: "NExT (Ni et al., 2024) uses self-generated trajectories filtered by unit test correctness to self-evolve agents for program repair tasks." and "process reward models to detect and correct errors throughout the reasoning process, generally yielding better improvement than using outcome-level feedback."
  where: p.14-15

- claim: Self-play and proposer/solver setups remove external data (Absolute Zero, R-Zero).
  number: none
  setup: Section 4.1.1.
  quote: "Absolute Zero (Zhao et al., 2025a) trains a single model that alternates between task proposer and solver roles, self-evolving by generating and solving its own problems."
  where: p.14

- claim: The survey sorts prompt optimisers into four families: edit-based (GrIPS, TEMPERA), generative (APE, OPRO, MIPRO), text-gradient (ProTeGi, TextGrad), evolutionary (EvoPrompt, Promptbreeder). Its main taxonomy figures are Fig 4 (single-agent) and Fig 5 (all methods).
  number: 4 families
  setup: Section 4.2.
  quote: "ProTeGi (Pryzant et al., 2023) generates text gradients by criticising the current prompt."
  where: p.15-17

- claim: Reflexion (episodic reflection stored as memory) and AWM, A-MEM, Mem0, MEM1 are the memory-evolution examples. These are descriptions, not results.
  number: none
  setup: Section 4.3.
  quote: "Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023) enables agents to reflect on task feedback and store episodic insights, promoting self-improvement over time."
  where: p.18

- claim: ADAS, Meta Agent Search, represents prompts, workflows and tool use as Python code. This lets a meta-agent rewrite the agent's own logic.
  number: none
  setup: Section 5.2.3.
  quote: "ADAS (Hu et al., 2025a) pioneered this approach through its Meta Agent Search framework, representing prompts, workflows, and tool use as Python code to enable iterative agent generation and evaluation."
  where: p.25

- claim: One of only two quantitative claims in the survey: OPTIMA reports a large gain at low token cost.
  number: 2.8x performance gain at under 10% of token cost
  setup: OPTIMA (Chen et al. 2025h), multi-agent communication training via SFT/DPO/hybrid. Tasks needing intensive information exchange. The survey does not give the benchmark or baseline. It is the cited paper's claim.
  quote: "It reports a 2.8× performance gain with less than 10% of the token cost on tasks demanding intensive information exchange"
  where: p.26, ~chars 117,500

- claim: A well-prompted single LLM can match complex multi-agent discussion on some reasoning benchmarks. This is evidence that added structure is not always worth it.
  number: none
  setup: Section 5.1, citing Pan et al. 2025a.
  quote: "single large LLMs with well-crafted prompts can match the performance of complex multi-agent discussion frameworks on multiple reasoning benchmarks (Pan et al., 2025a)"
  where: p.23

- claim: Confidence-gated debate cuts cost without hurting performance. This is relevant to trigger logic (run the expensive step only when needed).
  number: none ("sharply reduce")
  setup: Eo et al. 2025, cited.
  quote: "triggering multi-agent debates only when a single model exhibits low confidence can sharply reduce inference costs without hindering performance (Eo et al., 2025)."
  where: p.23

- claim: LLM-as-judge feedback is a proxy for the optimiser, with known weaknesses. Agent-as-a-Judge (Zhuge 2024b) judges whole trajectories and matched human experts better than LLM judges on DevAI. It is hard to generalise beyond code.
  number: none
  setup: Section 7.2. Source is cited, with no figures given.
  quote: "these methods are sensitive to prompt design and susceptible to biases introduced by subtle instructional variations" and "implementing the Agent-as-a-Judge methodology introduces additional complexity and raises challenges for generalisation to domains other than code generation."
  where: p.31-32

- claim: The survey ties evaluation to evolution: evaluation is the feedback mechanism, not an endpoint.
  number: none
  setup: Section 7 intro.
  quote: "Evaluation is no longer viewed as a static endpoint but as a dynamic feedback mechanism"
  where: p.30

- claim: Existing regulation assumes static models, so evolving agents need new audit mechanisms.
  number: none
  setup: Section 8.1.1.
  quote: "The dynamic nature of evolving agents undermines existing legal frameworks (e.g., EU AI Act, GDPR), which assume static models and fixed decision logic."
  where: p.32

LIMITS
- It is a literature survey with no experiments. It gives no evidence for the success rates, costs or failure rates of evolving loops. The only ratio, OPTIMA's, is second-hand.
- The authors concede that nearly all optimisation is text-only and assumes a fixed toolset. Tool creation is "still emerging". Multimodal and spatial evolution are open. Cost, latency and instability of multi-agent optimisation are unresolved.
- No discussion of the failure modes the note lists: invented improvements, state rot, compounding errors, scope limits. The nearest concern is reward instability and safety drift. It does not discuss "no-op" outcomes.
- Cutoff is mid-2025. Anything later, including the note's 2026 papers, is absent. The survey is mostly about optimising offline against benchmarks. It says little about production practice or weeks-long deployed loops.
- It cites Gao et al. 2025b as a concurrent survey, which it distinguishes by "what to evolve, when to evolve, and how to evolve".
- The abstract and conclusion name the framework's components "Inputs, Agent System, Objectives, and Optimisers", while Section 3 says "Environment" instead of "Objectives". This is a minor internal inconsistency.

BUILDS ON (as printed)
Reflexion (Shinn et al., 2023); STaR (Zelikman et al., 2022); OPRO (Yang et al., 2024a); TextGrad (Yuksekgonul et al., 2024); ProTeGi (Pryzant et al., 2023); EvoPrompt (Guo et al., 2024b); Promptbreeder (Fernando et al., 2024); ADAS (Hu et al., 2025a); AFlow (Zhang et al., 2025j); DSPy (Singhvi et al., 2023); MIPRO (Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024); Self-Refine (Madaan et al., 2023); Agent-as-a-Judge (Zhuge et al., 2024b); DeepSeek-R1 (Guo et al., 2025); Absolute Zero (Zhao et al., 2025a); R-Zero (Huang et al., 2025); AlphaEvolve is cited as "Novikov et al., 2025". The Three Laws are modelled on Asimov's.

CODE: none (no code in the paper). Only the formula "A∗ = arg max A∈S O(A; I), (1)", on p.11.

FIGURES (from text only; I did not run the figure script)
- Fig 1, p.2: LLM learning moving from static data to interaction to lifelong self-evolution. Useful for the MOP to MASE path.
- Table 1, p.4: compares MOP, MOA, MAO and MASE by feedback type. It states the paradigm shift fastest.
- Fig 3, p.10: the self-evolving loop (inputs, agent system, environment, optimiser). Its caption says "The optimiser updates the agent system through a defined search space and optimisation algorithm until performance goals are met." It is the survey's best single-image match to the note's fast-loop/slow-loop picture.
- Fig 5, p.13: full taxonomy tree of methods. Fig 2, p.5: 2023-2025 timeline of methods.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. Figure text is garbled in extraction (Fig 2 and Fig 3 are mixed word lists), but this does not affect any claim. Page numbers are from the printed footers, and character offsets are approximate.
